tools.description: Census of AI detections across the customer's AI agent sessions: every AI detection rule that has fired, by human-readable name, with the number of DISTINCT SESSIONS each fired in. Use this for "which AI detections have fired", "what AI detections do we have", "most common AI detection", or any question about how widespread a detection is — it answers in one call. Do NOT answer those by paging search_ai_sessions and counting: that can be hundreds of thousands of rows and will not give the right number anyway. session_count is DISTINCT SESSIONS, never occurrences — a rule that fired 40 times in one session counts once, because detections are re-emitted on a timer and occurrence counts are inflated. The counts do NOT sum to the session total: one session can fire several rules, so adding them double-counts. Always read them against the two denominators in the response: sessions_with_detections (sessions carrying at least one AI detection) and sessions_total (all sessions in scope) — typically only a small percentage of sessions carry any AI detection, so a bare count reads as a fleet-wide problem when it is a small subset. Only ENABLED detection rules appear; a rule retired from the rule library is excluded so it never reads as live coverage. Covers runtime session detections only — scanner-sourced AI findings carry no session and are not represented here (use search_ai_security_risks for those). To see the actual sessions behind any row, call search_ai_sessions with detection_id set to that row's detection_id — and pass the SAME recency_days you used here, or the two will disagree because one is windowed and the other is not. With matching windows the number of sessions it returns equals session_count exactly. Optionally narrow with hostname/agent/classification/severity, a recency_days window, and/or the asset scope (asset_tags, asset_importance, asset_type) — every filter narrows the counts and the denominators together.

agent.description: Only count sessions for this agent (partial, case-insensitive, e.g. 'claude code', 'cursor')

asset_importance.description: Scope to assets in these Business Impact tiers: 1=critical, 2=high, 3=medium, 4=low, 5=minimal. "Highest-priority" or "most critical" assets = [1] (optionally [1,2]).

asset_importance_op.description: How to match asset_importance: equals (default) or notEqual.

asset_tags.description: Scope results to assets carrying these tags. Use the tag names exactly as the user refers to them (e.g. "Production", "PCI", "APAC"); do not invent tags. Up to 25.

asset_tags_op.description: How to match asset_tags: equals = assets WITH any of these tags (default); notEqual = assets WITHOUT them (assets with no tags at all also match notEqual).

asset_type.description: Scope to a single asset type (workstation or server).

asset_type_op.description: How to match asset_type: equals (default) or notEqual.

classification.description: Only count sessions with this classification (partial, case-insensitive, e.g. 'coding', 'autonomous')

hostname.description: Only count sessions on hosts matching this hostname (partial, case-insensitive)

recency_days.description: Only count sessions active in the last N days. Omit for all history — note that unbounded includes sessions from months ago, so for "what is firing now" pass a window such as 30.

severity.description: Only count sessions whose highest detection severity is this level

tools.name: count_ai_session_detections

tools.description: Census of secret detectors in the customer's environment: every kind of secret the Spektion scanner has found, with how many findings and how many DISTINCT ASSETS each appears on. Use this for "what kinds of secret do we have", "which secrets are most widespread", "break down our secrets by type", or any question about the shape of the secret population — it answers in one call. Do NOT answer those by paging search_secrets and counting: it returns at most 100 findings per page and a tenant can hold tens of thousands, so a client-side tally is a sample presented as a total. finding_count is FINDINGS, one per detector-and-file-location, NOT distinct credentials: the same key in two files counts twice. asset_count is DISTINCT ASSETS. The two answer different questions and neither is the other. The rows do NOT sum to findings_total: findings whose detector is not fully identified (no name, or no id to drill down by) contribute to findings_total while producing no row, so a gap between the two is that population and not an error. Separately, the asset_count column does not sum to assets_with_findings either, because one asset carries several detectors and is counted once per detector. Always read the counts against the denominators in the response: assets_with_findings (assets carrying at least one secret), assets_scanned_for_secrets (assets whose latest secret scan ran at all) and assets_total (every asset in scope). Secret scanning is OPT-IN and typically covers a small fraction of the fleet, so a bare count reads as a fleet-wide inventory when it describes a sample — and the gap between assets_scanned_for_secrets and assets_total is exactly the population where a zero means "never looked", not "clean". To see the individual findings behind any row, call search_secrets with detector_id set to that row's detector_id — NOT detector_name, which is a substring match and will also return other detectors whose names contain this one's (asking for "Connection String" also returns "Azure Connection String"). Pass the SAME hostname/asset_id AND the same asset scope you used here, or the two will disagree — both queries apply all of them at the same gate, so the counts match exactly only when both calls carry the same ones. With the id and matching filters, the number of findings search_secrets reports equals this row's finding_count exactly. Narrow with hostname, asset_id, and/or the asset scope (asset_tags, asset_importance, asset_type); every one of them moves the counts AND the denominators together, so a scoped census reports that scope's coverage rather than the fleet's. When the result is empty, read the message field: an empty census means "nobody has scanned" far more often than it means "nothing is there", and those are opposite conclusions. If truncated is true the detector list was cut at group_limit and detectors_total says how many exist.

asset_id.description: Only count findings on this asset (exact match). Use the asset_id field from search_assets, not the hostname.

asset_importance.description: Scope to assets in these Business Impact tiers: 1=critical, 2=high, 3=medium, 4=low, 5=minimal. "Highest-priority" or "most critical" assets = [1] (optionally [1,2]).

asset_importance_op.description: How to match asset_importance: equals (default) or notEqual.

asset_tags.description: Scope results to assets carrying these tags. Use the tag names exactly as the user refers to them (e.g. "Production", "PCI", "APAC"); do not invent tags. Up to 25.

asset_tags_op.description: How to match asset_tags: equals = assets WITH any of these tags (default); notEqual = assets WITHOUT them (assets with no tags at all also match notEqual).

asset_type.description: Scope to a single asset type (workstation or server).

asset_type_op.description: How to match asset_type: equals (default) or notEqual.

hostname.description: Only count findings on hosts matching this hostname (partial, case-insensitive). Two characters are wildcards rather than literals: _ matches any single character and % matches any sequence, so a term containing them matches more broadly than it reads (searching prod_db also matches prod-db). This is how every hostname filter in the product behaves.

tools.name: count_secrets_by_detector

tools.description: List the compiled artifacts (binaries) an AI agent session produced, one entry per (binary, path) the session wrote. NOTE this is not a count of distinct binaries: the same binary written to two paths is two entries and counts twice in total_count, which on real data inflates the number by up to 2.6x (one dev session reports 226 entries over 86 distinct binaries). Say "wrote N build outputs", or count the distinct hash values yourself, rather than reporting total_count as the number of programs the agent built. Use this whenever the question is WHAT an agent built or compiled — "what did this session compile", "name the binaries this agent produced", "where was it written" — because the session record itself carries only a metric_compilers count, not the artifacts behind it. Returns per artifact: hash, linked_to_executable, name, path, language, compiler_path, size_bytes, asset_id, hostname, platform, asset_importance (Business Impact tier, 1 critical … 5 minimal), first_compiled_at, last_compiled_at and detail_url, plus total_count (artifacts matching THIS call, including any language filter, before paging, so it equals the session's total only when language is omitted; the payload echoes language_filter whenever one was applied), returned, offset, limit, max_limit and truncated. The page is capped at 100 artifacts (default 25) — one build can produce hundreds — so when truncated is true, page with offset rather than reporting the page as the whole. truncated means "more artifacts follow this page", so it is false on the last page and past the end — compare total_count with offset + returned to place a page in the whole. The hash is the same identifier search_executables returns and get_executable_details accepts, so an artifact can drill through to what the binary did once it ran. Drill through with get_executable_details, which takes a hash and is on both surfaces; search_executables has NO hash input, so a hash passed to it is ignored and the page that comes back describes other binaries entirely. Rows carry Spektion's XXH3 hash only — there is no hash_md5 here, which is a decision rather than an oversight: an MD5 is recorded against executables observed on an asset, and most build outputs never run there, so the field would be empty far more often than useful. When a row's linked_to_executable is true and the caller needs an MD5 to pivot into an outside tool, pass its hash to get_executable_details, which returns hash_md5 for it (empty when unknown or metadata is not yet available). Check linked_to_executable on the row before drilling through: it is true only when the hash resolves on the executables surface. Most build outputs never execute, so false is the ordinary case (911 of 5,425 hashes resolve on dev, 206 of 1,004 on prod, measured 2026-09-24) and means "this build output was never seen running", not that the hash is wrong — do not present a false as a missing record or retry the lookup. IMPORTANT, and the reason an empty list is not self-explanatory: this population is the compilation evidence the sensor hashed, and an artifact that never got a hash never enters it. The artifacts_state field types the empty case for you — artifacts_listed, compiler_activity_without_recorded_artifacts (the session ran compilers but Spektion cannot name what they produced — do NOT report this as "it compiled nothing"), no_compiler_activity_recorded, session_not_found, no_artifacts_matching_filter (a language filter matched nothing — this says nothing about what the session built, so re-run without the filter before concluding anything), artifact_absence_unexplained (the session record could not be read, so the empty list is unexplained rather than meaningful), or invalid_session_id (nothing was looked up at all). Requires session_id: the UUID from search_ai_sessions.

language.description: Only artifacts whose source language matches exactly, e.g. 'rust', 'go', 'cpp', 'cs', 'java', 'swift'. Omit for all languages; an unknown label matches nothing rather than failing.

limit.description: Page size — max artifacts to return (default 25, max 100)

offset.description: Pagination offset — number of artifacts to skip (default 0). Use with total_count to page through a large build.

session_id.description: AI session UUID to list artifacts for (from search_ai_sessions results)

tools.name: get_ai_session_artifacts

tools.description: Get a single asset's full profile by hostname: the asset summary (same fields as search_assets — exposure score/severity, Business Impact tier, online status, counts, and runtime risks), plus the list of installed software (name, publisher, used/unused, versions, grade, score) and observed network activity (software_name, destination, activity, observation_count, is_internal). Also returns secret_count — how many secret findings (hardcoded credentials, API keys, tokens) the Spektion scanner recorded in this asset's LATEST secret scan. The grain is FINDINGS, one per detector-and-location, NOT distinct credentials: the same key in two files counts twice. It is exactly the number of findings search_secrets holds for that asset — call search_secrets with asset_id (the asset_id field on this result, not the hostname — a hostname filter matches partially and pulls in other assets) and read its total_count (its items array is capped by limit) for the individual findings and their file locations. A 0 is NOT evidence that an asset holds no secrets: secret scanning is an opt-in scan type most assets have never run, and 0 means "never secret-scanned" and "scanned, clean" equally — the two are not distinguishable from this number, and no per-asset was-it-scanned signal exists today. A removed (tombstoned) sensor also reports 0 while its other counts may linger for one cache cycle. So describe a 0 as "no secret findings recorded", never as "clean". Also returns secret_types — the deduplicated detector names of the secrets found in this asset's LATEST secret scan ("SSH Private Key", "JWT Token", "AWS Secret Access Key"). These are exactly the values search_secrets returns in each finding's detector_name field — NOT its rule_name, which is the same constant string on every secret finding — so cross-reference them against detector_name. It is types-PRESENT, not a count of credentials: an asset with 2 SSH keys and 5 JWTs lists each name once; use search_secrets with asset_id for the individual findings and their file locations. An EMPTY array means the latest secret scan reported no named types, which covers a clean asset, an asset never secret-scanned, and an asset whose every finding came from one of the few detectors that report no name (some SSH-key and AWS-key rules among them) — so an empty secret_types is never evidence that the asset is clean. The field is ABSENT rather than empty when the lookup did not answer: absent means unknown, not zero. Only get_asset_details reports secret_types; search_assets rows carry secret_count only. secret_count and secret_types describe the same scan and the same findings, so a positive count with an EMPTY secret_types is a real state (every finding came from a detector that reports no name) — it is not a contradiction and not a clean asset. Requires an exact hostname (use search_assets first to resolve it).

hostname.description: Exact asset hostname (case-insensitive). Use search_assets to resolve the hostname first.

tools.name: get_asset_details

tools.description: List the executables currently present on a specific asset by hostname, most recently seen first. Returns, per executable: hash, hash_md5 (empty when unknown or metadata is not yet available), the path it was last observed at on this asset, the canonical software it is linked to (software_id, software_name; absent when unlinked), first_seen and last_seen on this asset, execution_count on this asset, signing status (is_signed, is_trusted), detection_count and detection_categories, and detail_url. path, first/last seen and execution_count are specific to this asset. is_signed, is_trusted, detection_count and detection_categories are attributes of the hash across every asset that observed it, so a detection listed here may have fired on a different asset: to see which hosts a detection fired on, call get_executable_details with the hash. Requires hostname (use search_assets first to find it). Page with offset: advance it by the echoed limit while truncated is true, and dedupe by hash, because the asset's executables can change between pages. Use this to answer questions like 'what is running on this host' or 'show me unsigned executables on SERVER01' -- unsigned is is_signed=false, and a row with is_trusted=true but no certificate is still labelled Unsigned; on macOS it is usually ad-hoc code.

hostname.description: Asset hostname to look up (partial match supported)

offset.description: Number of results to skip, for pagination (default 0)

tools.name: get_asset_executables

tools.description: Get the Spektion-specific preventative and detective controls associated with a runtime detection (runtime weakness / risk) — the hardening and monitoring guidance shown on the /risks detail page's Controls tabs. Call this BEFORE offering any hardening or monitoring advice for a runtime weakness. Identify the detection by detection_id (the id/risk_id from search_detections or get_detection_events). Returns preventive_controls (each with title, description, effectiveness, effort), vendor_fix_only, detective_control (a Spektion-provided Sigma detection rule), and detective_control_error. Report ONLY what this tool returns; do not supply your own generic hardening or monitoring guidance to fill a gap. When preventive_controls is empty, say Spektion has no preventive control on file and stop. When vendor_fix_only is true (set only when there are no preventive controls), Spektion has determined there is NO client-side preventive control and remediation requires a vendor patch — report that and do not offer hardening steps as a fix. When detective_control is null, Spektion has no detective control for this detection — say so and stop. When detective_control_error is set, the detective control could not be retrieved right now (a temporary failure, not absence) — tell the user it is temporarily unavailable and to try again, and do not claim Spektion has none. Never present anything as a Spektion control that this tool did not return.

detection_id.description: Detection/risk id from search_detections or get_detection_events (e.g. "DET-00007").

tools.name: get_detection_controls

tools.description: Get evidence summaries behind a runtime detection (runtime weakness). Use this tool when asked to show the evidence, events, or logs for a runtime weakness or risk; never route those requests to search_ai_security_risks, which covers the separate AI-security surface. Identify the detection by detection_id when available, or name to resolve it; ambiguous names return candidates so you can retry with a specific ID. Returns software-product groups, not individual events: one row per affected product plus one unattributed group when present. total_count counts these groups. first_seen is the earliest detection time for the group. process_path, module_name, api_function_name when available, and outputs provide evidence; payload fields are selected independently from latest events and can describe different events when latest timestamps tie. A row with unattributed=true combines evidence from executables not linked to a product, can represent thousands of executables, and must never be described as one program; it has no software_id. Rows are ordered by first_seen, newest first. Page with limit (default 20, max 100) and offset (default 0, maximum 4294967295); advance offset by the limit used until offset + returned reaches total_count. truncated=true means groups remain after this nonempty page. Stop advancing on an empty page and read message when present. An empty nonzero-offset page probes the total; if that probe fails, total_count=0 is unknown, not evidence of no matches. If the probe sees groups beyond an empty page, message directs you to restart at offset 0 instead of continuing the walk. Live data can shift page boundaries, causing repeated or missed groups; there is no snapshot guarantee. Each page recomputes the detection's history, so fetch only as far as the question needs.

detection_id.description: Detection/risk id from search_detections (or the risk_id field on assets and software). Preferred when known.

limit.description: Max software-product groups to return (default 20, max 100)

name.description: Detection name to resolve (partial case-insensitive match). Used when detection_id is not known.

offset.description: Number of results to skip, for pagination (default 0, maximum 4294967295). Page by advancing it until offset + returned reaches total_count.

tools.name: get_detection_events

tools.description: Get detailed information about a specific executable by hash. Returns the executable summary (hash_md5 — empty when unknown or metadata is not yet available, filenames, signing/trust status, platform, asset count, detection count) plus observed file paths with full code-signing certificate details (subject, issuer, fingerprint, validity dates, self-signed flag), associated runtime detections (name, category, severity, asset count), and endpoints where the executable is present (hostname, importance tier). Requires the executable hash (use search_executables first to find it). Optionally scope it with asset_tags, asset_importance and/or asset_type, the same filters search_executables takes: paths, endpoints and detections then cover in-scope assets only, and a detection's asset_count and first/last seen count only its triggers on those assets. Under a scope the summary's asset_count and detection_count are OMITTED, because they are fleet-wide totals with no scoped answer; filenames, platform, first/last seen and signing status stay fleet-wide attributes of the hash. A scoped call where the executable was never observed on an in-scope asset is not an error: the response carries applied_scope and a message — relay that, and do not say the executable is absent from the environment.

asset_importance.description: Scope to assets in these Business Impact tiers: 1=critical, 2=high, 3=medium, 4=low, 5=minimal. "Highest-priority" or "most critical" assets = [1] (optionally [1,2]).

asset_importance_op.description: How to match asset_importance: equals (default) or notEqual.

asset_tags.description: Scope results to assets carrying these tags. Use the tag names exactly as the user refers to them (e.g. "Production", "PCI", "APAC"); do not invent tags. Up to 25.

asset_tags_op.description: How to match asset_tags: equals = assets WITH any of these tags (default); notEqual = assets WITHOUT them (assets with no tags at all also match notEqual).

asset_type.description: Scope to a single asset type (workstation or server).

asset_type_op.description: How to match asset_type: equals (default) or notEqual.

hash.description: Executable hash identifier (e.g. from search_executables results)

tools.name: get_executable_details

tools.description: Get a high-level security posture overview from internal analytics routes: total assets, an active/stale/disabled asset breakdown (active = enabled and seen within the last 30 days (seen = any sensor check-in, not proof of live monitoring); stale = enabled but not seen in 30 days; disabled = not enabled, at the sensor level — per-asset scan enablement is a separate state this tool does not report — these three are disjoint and sum to total assets), assets by platform, total canonical software, software by platform, and vulnerability counts by severity. When available it also includes total runtime detections and the organizational exposure headline — org_exposure_score, org_exposure_severity, and org_exposure_delta (change vs the previous period; negative means improving). For a user whose access is limited to some assets, every count here covers only the assets they can access, org_exposure_delta is omitted, and the exposure headline is omitted when none of those assets has exposure data. Use this for 'how is my environment / security posture doing' overview questions before drilling into specific areas.
tools.name: get_security_posture

tools.description: Get details about specific software products matching a name: a risk summary plus the assets (endpoints) where each is installed. Returns, per matched product, a software summary (name, publisher, platform, score, severity, grade, present versions, CVE/detection counts, risk flags, network activity) and an assets array (hostname, ip_address, importance = Business Impact tier, usage_tracked, used, installed versions). CRITICAL for used/unused questions: usage_tracked=false means usage is not tracked for this product on that asset — usage is UNKNOWN, never report it as unused, and 'used' is omitted; only when usage_tracked=true is 'used' meaningful (true=used, false=genuinely unused). Requires software_name (partial, case-insensitive match; use search_software first to find the exact product). Matches up to 10 products; assets capped at 100 per product.
tools.name: get_software_details

tools.description: Get tenant configuration including SLA remediation policy, asset importance defaults, and KEV override settings.
tools.name: get_tenant_settings

tools.description: Look up a specific CVE via internal analytics routes. Always returns CVE ID, severity, CVSS score (score), Spektion risk score (risk_score, risk_severity, plus risk_score_min/risk_score_max for the spread across observed instances) when computed, KEV flag, platforms, first_seen, endpoint_count, detail_url, and impacted assets (hostname/platform). score is the industry CVSS rating; risk_score is Spektion's per-tenant runtime risk score — use risk_score (not score) for 'how risky is this CVE in our environment' questions. Also returns sla_due_date and sla_status (overdue, due_today, due_soon, on_track), computed server-side against the tenant SLA matrix and the real current date — use sla_status directly for overdue questions. Optional enriched fields (description, EPSS, exploit status, remote exploitability, is_used, type, CWEs, os_impacted, impacted software, asset importance, cvss_vector — the raw CVSS vector string like 'CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/...') come from cache and may be missing or stale.

tools.description: Search AI security detections for the /ai-security surface only, paginated and ordered most-recent-first (last 90 days). Results combine runtime sensor detections (source=runtime) with scanner risk findings (source=scan) for AI/agent activity. Filters (hostname, asset_id, severity, rule_name, source) are applied server-side. Returns items plus total_count (total matches before paging), returned (this page's size), and offset — page through large result sets with limit + offset. Each item has event_id, event_time, source, rule_id, rule_name, severity, hostname, platform, asset_id, cvss_v31_score, cvss_v40_score, process_path (when present), matched_params (when present), and detail_url. sort_by=severity reorders the returned page most-severe-first. This is NOT the source for runtime-weakness (/risks) evidence.

limit.description: Page size — max results to return (default 20, max 100)

rule_name.description: Filter by rule name (partial case-insensitive match)

tools.description: Search AI agent session summaries across the customer's environment, paginated and ordered most-recent-first. Returns session_id, hostname, platform, asset_id, agent, classification, severity_max, started_at, duration, is_interim, metric_processes, metric_connections, metric_detections, metric_risk_flags, metric_file_writes, detections (when present; each with id and human-readable name — report the names, not the DET-AI-#### codes), risk_flags (when present), and detail_url, plus total_count (total matches before paging), returned (this page's size), and offset. All metric_* fields are aggregate counts, not itemized data; on the chat surface, get_ai_session_details returns the full metric set for a session (that tool is chat-only, so it is not available over MCP). For what a session COMPILED, get_ai_session_artifacts names the binaries it produced per artifact, on both surfaces. Filters (hostname, asset_id, agent, classification, severity) are applied server-side. Sort by duration or detection_count. Page through large result sets with limit + offset. Optionally scope the search to a subset of the fleet with asset_tags (operational tags like "Production"/"PCI", names as the user says them), asset_importance (Business Impact tiers 1=critical … 5=minimal), and/or asset_type (workstation/server) — use these for questions like "AI sessions on my production-tagged assets" or "agent sessions on my critical servers". They narrow which assets' sessions are returned. A scope that matches no assets is not an error: the response then carries applied_scope alongside an empty list and a message — relay that, do not report it as "there are no AI sessions".

asset_importance.description: Scope to assets in these Business Impact tiers: 1=critical, 2=high, 3=medium, 4=low, 5=minimal. "Highest-priority" or "most critical" assets = [1] (optionally [1,2]).

asset_type.description: Scope to a single asset type (workstation or server).

asset_type_op.description: How to match asset_type: equals (default) or notEqual.

classification.description: Filter by session classification (partial case-insensitive match, e.g. 'coding', 'autonomous')

detection_id.description: Return only sessions in which at least ONE of these AI detection rules fired, e.g. ["DET-AI-1020"]. Several ids are OR, never AND — a session matches if any one of them fired, so this cannot express "fired both". Ids come from the detections[] on a session or from the AI-detection census; if the user names a detection in words ("credential file reads"), find its id first rather than guessing. An unknown id is not an error, it simply matches no sessions.

tools.description: Search assets (systems with a Spektion sensor). Returns hostname, IP, OS, domain, platform (windows/macos/linux), online status, enabled (sensor-level; per-asset scan enablement is a separate state not reported here), exposure score (0-100, higher = more exposed), exposure severity (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW), Business Impact tier (importance: 1=critical … 5=minimal, null=unassigned), first/last seen, last logged-on user, software/unused-software/detection/CVE/network-destination/executable counts, and an array of individual runtime risks (each with risk_id, risk_name, category, is_elevated, detail_url). Also returns secret_count — how many secret findings (hardcoded credentials, API keys, tokens) the Spektion scanner recorded in this asset's LATEST secret scan. The grain is FINDINGS, one per detector-and-location, NOT distinct credentials: the same key in two files counts twice. It is exactly the number of findings search_secrets holds for that asset — call search_secrets with asset_id (the asset_id field on this result, not the hostname — a hostname filter matches partially and pulls in other assets) and read its total_count (its items array is capped by limit) for the individual findings and their file locations. A 0 is NOT evidence that an asset holds no secrets: secret scanning is an opt-in scan type most assets have never run, and 0 means "never secret-scanned" and "scanned, clean" equally — the two are not distinguishable from this number, and no per-asset was-it-scanned signal exists today. A removed (tombstoned) sensor also reports 0 while its other counts may linger for one cache cycle. So describe a 0 as "no secret findings recorded", never as "clean". Filter by hostname, platform, or online status; sort by last_seen to surface not-recently-seen assets. For authoritative active/stale/disabled COUNTS use get_security_posture (server-side over the whole fleet) — this list is capped (max 100) and has no enabled filter, so do not tally disabled-vs-stale from it. Page the fleet with offset: advance it by the limit you used until offset + returned reaches total_count, and read offset back off each response. The page size is capped at 100 because each page also fetches that page's runtime risks in one batched lookup that analytics hard-caps at 1000 ids, and because a full fleet is tens of thousands of assets — page rather than asking for more. Page UNSORTED whenever you need every asset exactly once. Under any sort_by the rows that tie on the sort key are separated only by hostname, which is not unique, so a deep sorted walk can repeat some assets and skip others. Across large production fleets this is under ~2% of assets, but it is much higher on small or heavily re-imaged ones — up to ~70% on some — so do not treat the low figure as a general rate, and page unsorted whenever the count has to be exact. sort_by=last_seen carries a second, larger version of the same hazard: it orders by the live check-in time, which changes as sensors report in, so rows move between pages as the walk runs. The default (unsorted) order reads a snapshot that is frozen for the life of a 15-minute refresh cycle, so it is stable within a cycle; a walk that spans a refresh boundary can still see rows shift, and there is no way to detect that from the response. Result fields depend on the query: on a plain hostname/platform search, total_count is exact — including on a page past the end, which returns no items but still reports the real match count and says so in a message — and any sort_by ranking is fleet-wide, and truncated=true means only that assets remain after this page (advance offset); on an is_online search the filter runs over a bounded window, so total_count can understate the true match count, truncated=true means the returned set may be incomplete, scanned = rows examined in that window, window_incomplete=true on a page means that window did not reach every asset the server-side filters matched (total_count is then a bounded sample; both keys ride every page of such a walk, and their absence means the window covered every match), and offset pages within that window rather than the whole fleet. On an individual returned row the enabled field still distinguishes a disabled asset (enabled=false) from a stale-but-enabled one (enabled=true with an old last_seen; last_seen is any sensor check-in, not proof of live monitoring). Each result has a detail_url — present assets (and their risks) as linked lists. For a single asset's installed software and network activity, use get_asset_details. Scope the whole search to a subset of the fleet with asset_tags (operational tags like "Production"/"PCI", names as the user says them), asset_importance (Business Impact tiers 1=critical … 5=minimal), and/or asset_type (workstation/server) — use these for questions like "assets tagged production" or "my most critical servers".

asset_importance_op.description: How to match asset_importance: equals (default) or notEqual.

tools.description: Search runtime detections (risks) in the customer's environment. These are Spektion-unique telemetry, distinct from CVEs. Categories: Runtime Weaknesses (likely to become a CVE), Exploit Impact/Blast Radius (increases exposure if exploited), Remotely Exploitable (binds to sockets/accepts connections). Returns name, impact level, category, subcategory, platform, CVE likelihood, affected asset count, affected software count, and detail_url for direct navigation. Filter by name, category, impact, or platform, and use offset to page through results. Each result includes a detail_url — present detections as a linked list using name and detail_url. Scope the search to a subset of the fleet with asset_tags (operational tags like "Production"/"PCI", names as the user says them), asset_importance (Business Impact tiers 1=critical … 5=minimal), and/or asset_type (workstation/server) — use these for questions like "runtime risks on production-tagged assets". A scope narrows both which detections are listed (a detection present only on out-of-scope assets drops out entirely, rather than appearing with a zero count) AND the per-asset counts: endpoint_count, software_count and elevated_software_count then describe the scoped subset, not the fleet. elevated_software_count is how many software products ran the detection ELEVATED, and it is the reason highest_impact reads elevated: a zero there with an elevated impact would be contradictory, so read the two together. A scope does NOT narrow first_seen. first_seen is recorded per detection with the asset folded out, so it is when the detection was first seen anywhere in the fleet, not on the scoped assets; sort_by=first_seen and sort_by=last_seen therefore order a scoped list by fleet-wide timestamps — present that ordering as "most recently first detected in the environment", never "on these assets". highest_impact CAN change under a scope: it takes the rule's elevated impact only when an in-scope asset ran it elevated, so a detection may read High fleet-wide and Medium on a scoped subset -- report it as the impact on the scoped assets. Still reported under a scope, and unchanged by it: name, category, subcategory, platform, description and cve_likelihood are properties of the detection RULE, identical under any scope, so report them as facts about the detection rather than about the scoped assets. A detection_id from this tool stays valid under a scope, but get_detection_events is always fleet-wide and cannot be scoped, so never present its evidence as coming from the scoped assets. Never describe an unscoped number as scoped. A scope that matches no assets is not an error: the response then carries applied_scope alongside an empty list and a message — relay that message and say nothing matches the requested scope, never "there are no runtime detections".

asset_importance_op.description: How to match asset_importance: equals (default) or notEqual.

asset_tags.description: Scope results to assets carrying these tags. Use the tag names exactly as the user refers to them (e.g. "Production", "PCI", "APAC"); do not invent tags. Up to 25.

asset_tags_op.description: How to match asset_tags: equals = assets WITH any of these tags (default); notEqual = assets WITHOUT them (assets with no tags at all also match notEqual).

asset_type.description: Scope to a single asset type (workstation or server).

asset_type_op.description: How to match asset_type: equals (default) or notEqual.

highest_impact.description: Filter to detections whose returned highest_impact is exactly this level (case-insensitive). It filters the same value each result reports, so highest_impact=critical returns exactly the detections shown as Critical. Ask for one level per call: for "critical or high", call once with critical and once with high.

name.description: Filter by detection name (partial case-insensitive match)

offset.description: Number of results to skip, for pagination (default 0)

sort_by.description: Sort results descending by this field. Use first_seen for most recently first-detected and last_seen for most recently active.

tools.description: Search observed executables across the customer's environment via ClickHouse. Returns hash, hash_md5 (empty when unknown or metadata is not yet available), filenames, asset count, platform, signing status (is_signed, is_trusted), whether the executable is linked to canonical software, detection count, first/last seen, and detail_url. Also returns detection_categories (unique list of detection types such as runtime_weakness, exploit_impact, remotely_exploitable) and a detections array with per-detection details: name, category, severity, weakness_score, weakness_severity, and cve_likelihood. Use detection data to assess executable risk — factor weakness severity, detection categories, and CVE likelihood alongside signing status when ranking executables. Filter by platform, signing status, or software linkage, all applied server-side so total_count describes the filtered set. Sort to find most widespread or newest executables. Page the whole inventory with offset: advance it by the echoed limit until offset + returned reaches total_count, and read offset back off each response. total_count is every match, counted before the page is cut, and it stays correct on a page past the end, which returns no items and says so in a message. truncated=true means executables remain after this page. Every order is broken by hash, so WITHIN ONE SNAPSHOT of the list a walk neither repeats nor skips, under any sort_by. The list itself is rebuilt every 15 minutes (and a scoped list is computed live, so it can move between any two pages), and a walk that crosses a rebuild CAN repeat and skip: newly seen executables enter at the head of the default first_seen order and push unvisited rows past the offset already reached. The two cancel out — every skipped row is paid for by a repeated one — so the number of rows collected still equals total_count even when some are missing. Do not treat that arithmetic as proof of completeness: DEDUPE BY hash, and report the distinct count. sort_by=last_seen re-ranks every recently active executable to the head at each rebuild, so prefer the default order for an exhaustive walk and treat last_seen or asset_count as a way to see the top of a ranking rather than all of it. Page size is capped at 100 — read the limit and max_limit the response echoes, and advance offset by the limit that came back, not the one you asked for. On a deployment that predates server-side counting, total_count is OMITTED rather than reported as 0 and total_count_unavailable=true rides the response: the items are still correct, so page on truncated alone — advance offset while truncated is true and stop the first time it is absent. Do NOT stop because a page returned fewer items than the limit: returned counts the rows left after software-linkage filtering, so a short page can still be followed by more. get_executable_details drills into a specific hash for certificate info, paths, hosts and detections. On a scoped question, pass it the same asset_tags / asset_importance / asset_type so its paths, hosts and detections stay within the scope. Scope the search to a subset of the fleet with asset_tags (operational tags like "Production"/"PCI", names as the user says them), asset_importance (Business Impact tiers 1=critical … 5=minimal), and/or asset_type (workstation/server) — use these for questions like "executables on my critical servers". A scope narrows WHICH executables are listed (a hash observed only on out-of-scope assets drops out entirely, rather than appearing with a zero count) and asset_count, which then counts only the in-scope assets. Also returns compilation provenance: compiled_locally (a compile of this exact binary was observed in this environment), created_by_ai_session (one of those compiles ran inside an AI agent session) and ai_session_id (the most recent such session — pass it to get_ai_session_artifacts, available on every surface, to see everything that session built; get_ai_session_details gives the session itself but is chat-only, so do not name it unless it is in your tool list). READ A FALSE CAREFULLY: both booleans mean "no compilation evidence is recorded for this hash within the last year", which is NOT the same as "this binary was downloaded" or "no agent built it". Compiled-artifact collection is recent and not yet active for every tenant — on prod only 3 of the 10 tenants with AI compiler activity have any artifact evidence at all — so a false is routinely the absence of collection rather than the absence of a compile. Only a true is positive evidence. Provenance is keyed on the hash at tenant level, so it travels with a binary copied to another asset. Under a scope, detection_count, detection_categories, compiled_locally, created_by_ai_session, ai_session_id and the detections array are OMITTED from every row rather than returned fleet-wide: detections and compilation provenance are both recorded against the executable hash with no asset dimension, so this tool has no scoped answer for them. Their absence on a scoped result is expected and is not a sign that the executables are detection-free — if the user needs detection data, either call get_executable_details on a hash with the same scope (its detections are counted over in-scope assets only), or offer to re-run the search without the asset scope. filenames, platform, first_seen, last_seen, is_signed, is_trusted and is_linked_to_software are likewise fleet-wide attributes of the hash, aggregated over every asset that ever observed it. Never describe an unscoped number as scoped. SIGNING: is_signed and is_trusted are the two raw sensor flags. The console's Signature label is "Trusted" only when BOTH are set, "Signed" when is_signed alone is, and "Unsigned" whenever is_signed is false -- so is_signed=false does map to Unsigned, and is_trusted on its own does NOT mean trusted. On macOS is_trusted is a signature-validity check that AD-HOC code passes, so a Homebrew or `go install` binary can report is_trusted=true with no certificate at all. Such a row is still labelled Unsigned; it is USUALLY ad-hoc code, but certificate-signed code whose signing details could not be read lands in the same state, so do not tell the user a binary is ad-hoc on these two flags alone. A scope that matches no assets is not an error: the response then carries applied_scope alongside an empty list and a message — relay that message and say nothing matches the requested scope, never "no executables are present".

asset_importance_op.description: How to match asset_importance: equals (default) or notEqual.

tools.description: List the actual outbound network connections (destinations) and inbound port bindings (listeners) observed for a software product — the records behind the software detail page's Network Destinations tab, NOT the aggregate network_destination_count / network_listener_count that search_software reports. This is the right tool whenever the user asks which/what destinations, domains, or IPs a product talks to, or which ports it listens on. Per destination: software_name, hostname (the asset that made the connection), destination_value (the domain or IP), destination_type, port, activity_type, is_internal (true = internal/private destination), and connection_count. Per listener: software_name, hostname, bind_address, port, activity_type, and listener_count. Requires software_name (partial case-insensitive match, at least 3 characters; use search_software first if unsure of the exact name). limit defaults to 50, max 200 — when a list is capped at the limit the response says so. For precise totals use the network_destination_count / network_listener_count fields on search_software.

limit.description: Max records to return per list (default 50, max 200)

software_name.description: Software product name (partial match, at least 3 characters)

tools.description: Search secret detections (credentials, API keys, tokens, and other sensitive data) found in the customer's environment by the Spektion scanner. Returns event_id, event_time, detector_id, detector_name, detector_tags, hostname, platform, asset_id, matched_params (when present), outputs (when present), and detail_url. detector_name is the REAL detector that fired -- "SSH Private Key", "JWT Token", "AWS Secret Access Key", "Credentials in URL" and ~60 others -- and is the ONLY field that distinguishes one kind of secret from another. Report it as the type of secret found, and filter on it. rule_name and rule_id are the scanner's wrapper: on every finding from the current scanner they are the SAME constant ("Hardcoded Secret Detected" / "DET-SEC-0400"), as are severity, category and subcategory. A small number of older findings predate that wrapper and carry their real detector in those columns instead -- detector_name already accounts for that, which is exactly why you read and filter detector_name and never rule_name. On a current-scanner finding none of those five carry information: never present them as the type of secret, never rank or group by them, and never conclude from a constant severity that findings are equally urgent. Filter by hostname, asset_id, or detector_name (partial, case-insensitive: "aws" matches "AWS Secret Access Key" and "AWS Access Key ID"). rule_name is a DEPRECATED alias that filters detector_name -- it is accepted so existing callers keep working, and it does NOT match the constant. detector_name is populated on every finding. A detector_name filter that comes back empty means no finding of that kind is recorded, which is not proof the environment is clean: secret scanning is opt-in and most assets have never run one. detector_tags is the detector's family (for example ["api","cloud","aws"] or ["crypto","ssh"]). Each finding's file location is in outputs.file_path and outputs.line_number. The grain is FINDINGS, one per detector-and-location, NOT distinct credentials: the same key in two files is two findings. Results cover each asset's LATEST secret scan only, with no time window. Sort by event_time (most recent first, default) or detector_name. total_count is every match, counted server-side before the page is cut, and the items array holds at most limit (max 100) of them. Page by advancing offset by the limit you used until offset + returned reaches total_count; the order is stable across pages, so nothing is skipped or repeated. If you only need counts per kind of secret, call count_secrets_by_detector instead of paging -- it answers in one call. The asset scope (asset_tags, asset_importance, asset_type) narrows which assets are searched, and total_count is counted after it is applied.

asset_tags.description: Scope results to assets carrying these tags. Use the tag names exactly as the user refers to them (e.g. "Production", "PCI", "APAC"); do not invent tags. Up to 25.

asset_tags_op.description: How to match asset_tags: equals = assets WITH any of these tags (default); notEqual = assets WITHOUT them (assets with no tags at all also match notEqual).

asset_type_op.description: How to match asset_type: equals (default) or notEqual.

detector_id.description: Filter by the detector's exact id, e.g. "SEC-CRYPTO-001". This is the drill-through key from count_secrets_by_detector: pass a census row's detector_id here and you get exactly the findings that row counted. detector_name is a substring match and will not reproduce a row when one detector name contains another.

detector_name.description: Filter by the real detector name, e.g. "SSH Private Key", "JWT Token", "AWS Secret Access Key" (partial, case-insensitive substring match). Two characters are wildcards rather than literals: _ matches any single character and % matches any sequence, so a term containing them matches more broadly than it reads (searching SSH_Private_Key also matches "SSH-Private-Key"). Use detector_id instead when you need the exact findings behind a count_secrets_by_detector row — a substring name match also returns detectors whose names contain this one's.

hostname.description: Filter by hostname (partial case-insensitive match). Two characters are wildcards rather than literals: _ matches any single character and % matches any sequence, so a term containing them matches more broadly than it reads (searching prod_db also matches prod-db). This is how every hostname filter in the product behaves.

offset.description: Number of results to skip, for pagination (default 0). Page by advancing it until offset + returned reaches total_count.

sort_by.description: Sort results: event_time (most recent first, default) or detector_name (alphabetical, groups findings by kind of secret)

tools.description: Search canonical installed software products across all assets using internal analytics routes (legacy software is excluded). Returns name, publisher, platform, endpoint count, unused endpoint count, present version count, CVE count, detection count, elevated detection count, has_elevated_risk, network activity (network destination/listener counts, makes_network_connection), and detail_url, all from internal analytics. score/severity are the software rollup score (higher = riskier) and its severity label, from a separate best-effort fetch that may be missing. grade, risk flags (has_high_risks, has_runtime_weakness, has_remote_exploitability), exploit_impacts, and the individual runtime risks array are enrichments computed from PostgreSQL category/score data and the risk library; a PostgreSQL enrichment failure fails the call, while risk-library data (risk flags, exploit_impacts, risks) is best-effort and is silently omitted when the library is unavailable. On the storeless MCP lane category/grade come from the tenant software cache, and are omitted if that fetch fails. Filter by name, platform, or category. Use sort_by for ranking questions, and offset to page through results. Use get_software_details to see which specific assets have a product — but ONLY on an unscoped question: get_software_details is always fleet-wide and cannot be scoped, so never pair its asset list with a scoped answer here. IMPORTANT: When the user asks about runtime risks, detections, or weaknesses for software, present individual risks from the risks array as a linked list using detail_url and risk_name. Scope the search to a subset of the fleet with asset_tags (operational tags like "Production"/"PCI", names as the user says them), asset_importance (Business Impact tiers 1=critical … 5=minimal), and/or asset_type (workstation/server) — use these for questions like "software installed on production-tagged assets". A scope narrows both which products are listed (a product present only on out-of-scope assets drops out entirely, rather than appearing with a zero count) AND their per-asset counts: endpoint_count, unused_endpoint_count, present_versions and cve_count then describe the scoped subset, not the fleet. detection_count, elevated_detection_count and has_elevated_risk narrow too, but only by RULE SET — they count the detection rules that apply to the software versions present on the in-scope assets, NOT detections observed on those assets — so say "N detection rules apply to the versions on these assets", never "N detections on these assets"; and "elevated" is a property of a rule observed anywhere in the fleet, so never "N elevated detections on these assets" either. A scope does NOT narrow network_destination_count, network_listener_count or makes_network_connection: network activity is recorded per (tenant, software) with no asset dimension, so all three still describe the WHOLE environment even when the row itself is in scope — never report them as the scoped figure, and if asked for network activity within a scope, say it is not available at that granularity. Still reported under a scope, and unchanged by it: score, severity, grade, has_high_risks, has_runtime_weakness, has_remote_exploitability, exploit_impacts and risks are product-level attributes identical under any scope, so report them as facts about the product, not about the scoped assets. Never describe an unscoped number as scoped. A scope that matches no assets is not an error: the response then carries applied_scope alongside an empty list and a message — relay that message and say nothing matches the requested scope, never "no software is installed".

tools.description: Search CVE vulnerabilities across the customer's environment using internal analytics routes. Always returns CVE ID, severity, CVSS score (score), Spektion risk score (risk_score) and risk_severity when computed, KEV flag, platforms, first_seen, affected asset count, and detail_url. score is the industry CVSS rating; risk_score is Spektion's per-tenant runtime risk score and is the right field for 'riskiest CVE in our environment' questions. Additional fields (EPSS score, exploit status, remote exploitability, is_used, published date, ransomware association, title) come from the analytics enriched response and may be missing. sla_due_date and sla_status (overdue, due_today, due_soon, on_track) are computed server-side against the tenant SLA matrix and the real current date — for 'past SLA / overdue' questions use sla_status directly rather than comparing dates yourself. Filter by name (CVE ID substring), severity, KEV, SLA status, platform, exploit_maturity, has_remote_exploitability, and is_used — all applied server-side over the whole environment (or over the whole asset scope, when one is set), so compound filters (e.g. used AND remotely exploitable AND actively exploited) return the exact matching set, not a sample. Sort to answer questions like 'which CVEs are actively used' or 'which CVEs are remotely exploitable'. For 'newest' CVE questions use published (when available); for most recently observed in this environment use first_seen. Use offset to page through results. Use get_vulnerability_details to see full details and impacted assets for a specific CVE — but ONLY on an unscoped question: get_vulnerability_details is always fleet-wide and cannot be scoped, so its endpoint_count and impacted-asset list will disagree with a scoped answer here and must never be presented as the in-scope hosts. Scope the search to a subset of the fleet with asset_tags (operational tags like "Production"/"PCI", names as the user says them), asset_importance (Business Impact tiers 1=critical … 5=minimal), and/or asset_type (workstation/server) — use these for questions like "open CVEs on assets tagged production". The scope narrows by ASSET, and severity, kev, exploit_maturity, has_remote_exploitability, is_used and sla_status still select the CVE — different grains, so keep them apart. A scope changes which CVEs are listed (a CVE open only on out-of-scope assets drops out entirely, rather than appearing with a zero count) AND every per-asset figure on the row: endpoint_count, first_seen, platforms, is_used, has_remote_exploitability, risk_score, risk_severity, sla_due_date and sla_status are then computed over the in-scope assets only, and total_count is the scoped match count. So "critical CVEs on production-tagged assets" means CVEs whose own severity is critical AND that are open on at least one in-scope asset. Still reported under a scope, and unchanged by it: cve_id, name, severity, score, epss_score, exploit_maturity, kev, kev_ransomware_campaign_use and published are properties of the CVE in the public catalog, identical under any scope — report them as facts about the CVE, never as findings about the scoped assets. detail_url likewise opens the fleet-wide CVE page, which does not carry the asset scope. Never describe an unscoped number as scoped. A scope that matches no assets is not an error: the response then carries applied_scope alongside an empty list and a message — relay that message and say nothing matches the requested scope, never "no vulnerabilities exist".

asset_importance.description: Scope to assets in these Business Impact tiers: 1=critical, 2=high, 3=medium, 4=low, 5=minimal. "Highest-priority" or "most critical" assets = [1] (optionally [1,2]).

asset_importance_op.description: How to match asset_importance: equals (default) or notEqual.

asset_tags.description: Scope results to assets carrying these tags. Use the tag names exactly as the user refers to them (e.g. "Production", "PCI", "APAC"); do not invent tags. Up to 25.

asset_tags_op.description: How to match asset_tags: equals = assets WITH any of these tags (default); notEqual = assets WITHOUT them (assets with no tags at all also match notEqual).

asset_type.description: Scope to a single asset type (workstation or server).

asset_type_op.description: How to match asset_type: equals (default) or notEqual.

exploit_maturity.description: Filter by exploit status: 'actively exploited' (seen exploited in the wild / CISA-KEV class), 'weaponized poc' (weaponized proof-of-concept), 'proof of concept' (PoC-only), or 'no known exploit'. The raw response codes (wild / poc-weaponized / poc / none) are also accepted.

has_remote_exploitability.description: Filter to only remotely exploitable CVEs (true) or not (false)

is_used.description: Filter by software usage status (true = used/running software, false = unused/installed-only)

kev.description: Filter by CISA KEV status (true = only KEV, false = only non-KEV)

limit.description: Max results per page (default 20, max 100). A 'both'-type CVE (affecting OS and software) is returned as two adjacent rows, so returned rows can exceed the backend page size. total_count counts backend (CVE identifier, vulnerability type) matches, not distinct CVE IDs or split display rows. Advance offset by the backend page size (at most 100), not by the number of display rows.

name.description: Filter to CVEs whose ID matches this substring (case-insensitive, server-side), e.g. 'CVE-2024-23222' or '23222'.

offset.description: Number of results to skip, for pagination (default 0)

platform.description: Filter to CVEs affecting a specific platform

sla_status.description: Filter by one SLA status before pagination using the tenant policy and current UTC date. Comma-separated statuses are not supported.

sort_by.description: Sort results descending by this field. risk_score is Spektion runtime risk; score is CVSS. Use 'published' for newest CVEs by disclosure date, 'first_seen' for most recently detected in this environment.
